front: What is a personal computer (PC)?
back: A general-purpose computing device designed for individual use, with a CPU, RAM, storage, and OS. It can run a wide range of software for tasks such as word processing, web browsing, and gaming.

front: What is a multifunctional device (MFD)?
back: An all-in-one machine that prints, scans, copies and faxes. 'MFD' means multifunctional device. It saves desk space and money compared to buying each machine separately.

front: Give three examples of mobile devices.
back: Smartphones, tablets, and laptops are all mobile devices. They are battery-powered, portable, and typically support wireless connectivity such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

front: What is a web server?
back: A web server is a computer that stores the files for a website. When someone visits the site, it sends the right web pages to their browser using HTTP or HTTPS.

front: Difference between a file server and an application server?
back: A file server is a shared hard drive that stores files so everyone on the network can open and save them. An application server runs a program centrally and sends the results out to users' computers.

front: Give two examples of entertainment systems and their uses.
back: Smart TVs stream on-demand video content via services such as Netflix. Games consoles (e.g. PlayStation, Xbox) provide interactive gaming and online multiplayer experiences.

front: What is an embedded system?
back: A small computer built into a bigger device to do one specific job. Examples: the control chip in a washing machine, a car's engine computer (ECU), and a smart thermostat.

front: What does IoT stand for, and what does it describe?
back: IoT stands for Internet of Things. It describes a network of physical objects embedded with sensors and software that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data, such as smart home devices and wearables.

front: How are IT systems used in manufacturing?
back: IT systems control robotic arms on assembly lines, monitor production quality via sensors, and manage stock levels through automated stock control. Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) uses software to control machinery directly.

front: Give two uses of IT systems in healthcare.
back: Electronic Patient Records (EPR) store and share patient data securely between NHS services. Diagnostic imaging systems (e.g. MRI scanners) use embedded computers to capture and analyse medical images.

front: What is a network diagram used for?
back: A network diagram is a drawing that shows how devices in a network are linked together. Standard symbols represent parts like routers, switches, servers and computers, so engineers can plan and record the setup.

front: Name the four standard flowchart symbols and their meanings.
back: Oval/terminator = start or end • Rectangle/process = an action or instruction • Diamond/decision = a yes/no question • Parallelogram/input-output = data entry or output. Arrows show the direction of flow.

front: What is a screen reader, and who benefits from it?
back: A screen reader is software that reads out loud what is on the screen (or turns it into braille). It helps people who are blind or have severe sight loss use a computer on their own.

front: What four characteristics are used to compare storage media?
back: Storage is compared by four things: Capacity (how much it holds) • Cost (price) • Speed (how fast it reads and writes) • Compatibility (whether it works with your device, e.g. USB or SATA).

front: Difference between manual and automatic data processing?
back: Manual processing needs a person at every step (e.g. typing data into a spreadsheet by hand). Automatic processing is done by hardware and software with no person involved (e.g. a sensor that logs temperatures by itself).

front: What is a real-time operating system (RTOS)?
back: A real-time operating system (RTOS) must respond within a strict time limit, so a job is never late. Examples: the system running an aircraft autopilot or a hospital monitor.

front: What is virtual memory?
back: Virtual memory is when the computer uses part of the hard drive as extra RAM when the real RAM is full. This lets larger programs run, but it is slower than real RAM.

front: Give three examples of utility software.
back: Antivirus software, disk defragmenters and file compression tools (like WinZip) are all utilities. Utility software does the 'housekeeping' jobs that keep the system running well.

front: What is a Command Line Interface (CLI)?
back: A Command Line Interface (CLI) is where you control the computer by typing text commands. It gives precise control and is fast for experts, but is harder to learn than clicking icons.

topic: A3.6 Open Source vs Proprietary Software
front: What is the key difference between open source and proprietary software?
back: Open source software lets anyone see and change the code (Linux, LibreOffice). Proprietary software is owned by a company and its code is kept secret (Windows, Adobe Photoshop).

front: What is the difference between a JPEG and a PNG image file?
back: JPEG shrinks photos by throwing away some detail to make files smaller (lossy) — best for photos. PNG keeps all detail and can have transparent backgrounds (lossless) — best for logos and diagrams.

front: What does 'downtime' mean in the context of implementing a new IT system?
back: Downtime is the time when an IT system is not working — for example while it is being replaced or updated. Organisations plan carefully to keep downtime short so they don't lose work or money.

front: How is an IT system used for stock control in retail?
back: Barcode or RFID scanners automatically update stock levels as items are sold or delivered. The system can automatically reorder when stock runs low, so the shop never runs out (and never orders too much).

front: Why do employees need initial and ongoing training when a new IT system is introduced?
back: Initial training makes sure staff can use the new system safely from day one. Ongoing training is needed because software keeps changing and new risks appear, so staff stay productive and safe.

front: Give two implications of artificial intelligence (AI) on IT system performance.
back: AI can improve performance by automating boring tasks and spotting faults before hardware breaks. But AI needs a lot of processing power and data, which increases energy and hardware demands.

front: What is Bluetooth, and what is its typical range?
back: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless link (about 10 metres) that connects nearby devices, like a phone to some headphones or a keyboard. It forms a personal area network (PAN).

front: What is Wi-Fi, and which IEEE standard defines it?
back: Wi-Fi is wireless networking that uses radio waves to connect devices to the internet. It follows the IEEE 802.11 standards (for example Wi-Fi 6 is also called 802.11ax).

front: What is Ethernet, and what are two advantages over Wi-Fi?
back: Ethernet is a wired connection using network cables (like Cat5e or Cat6). It is faster, more reliable and more secure than Wi-Fi because the signal can't be picked up through the air.

front: What is a star network topology?
back: A star topology connects every device to a central switch. If one device breaks, the rest keep working. The downside is that if the central switch fails, the whole network goes down.

front: Compare ring and bus network topologies.
back: Ring: each device connects to two others in a loop; a single break stops the whole network. Bus: all devices share one main cable; a break in that cable stops everything, and transmissions can clash.

front: What does PAN stand for, and give an example of its use?
back: PAN stands for Personal Area Network. It covers a very small area (about 10 metres) and connects personal devices, like a phone linked to Bluetooth headphones or a smartwatch.

front: What is a LAN?
back: A Local Area Network (LAN) connects devices in one building or campus. It is usually privately owned, uses Ethernet or Wi-Fi, and offers fast speeds with low delay.

front: Difference between a LAN and a WAN?
back: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area (one building or site) and is usually privately owned. A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a huge area — cities, countries or the whole world — often using the internet or leased lines, run by a telecoms provider.

front: What is a VPN and how does it protect data?
back: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) builds a secure, encrypted 'tunnel' between your device and a server over the internet. It hides your IP address and scrambles your data, so it can't be read or intercepted, and lets you safely reach the office network from home.

front: Give three factors affecting the choice of network for an organisation.
back: Cost (to set up and run) • Security (protecting data while it travels) • Scalability and whether it works with existing hardware and software. Organisations also think about downtime and the long-term effect on productivity.

front: What is the difference between POP3 and IMAP for email retrieval?
back: POP3 downloads emails to one device and usually removes them from the server. IMAP keeps emails on the server and syncs them across all your devices, so it's better if you check email on several devices.

front: What does SMTP stand for and what is it used for?
back: SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. It is used to send and pass on emails between mail servers. SMTP sends mail, while POP3 or IMAP receive it.

front: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
back: HTTP sends web page data as plain text, so it could be read by others. HTTPS adds encryption (TLS/SSL), scrambling data between the browser and server — shown by the padlock. HTTPS is needed for logins and online shopping.

front: What does TCP/IP stand for and what is its role?
back: TCP/IP is the set of rules that lets computers talk to each other over the internet. It packages data, gives it an address, sends it, and puts it back together at the other end.

front: What protocol is used to secure online payment transactions?
back: Online payments are protected with HTTPS/TLS encryption, plus extra checks like 3D Secure (a code from your bank) and tokenisation (a fake number is used instead of your real card number).

front: What is bandwidth?
back: Bandwidth is the most data that can travel over a connection in a set time, measured in megabits or gigabits per second (Mbps/Gbps). More bandwidth means more data can be sent at once.

front: What is latency and how does it affect network performance?
back: Latency is the delay between sending data and receiving it, measured in milliseconds (ms). High latency causes lag in video calls and online games, even when bandwidth is good.

front: What is the difference between MP3 and WAV audio formats?
back: MP3 shrinks music files by removing sounds you barely hear, so files are small — good for streaming. WAV is uncompressed with perfect quality but huge files — used in music production.

front: Give two common video file formats and describe their uses.
back: MP4 is widely used for streaming and sharing because it compresses well and plays on almost anything. AVI is an older Microsoft format with big files but high quality, still used in some video editing.

front: What is lossy compression?
back: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to make a file smaller. The removed data can't be recovered, so quality drops. Used for JPEG images, MP3 audio and MP4 video.

front: What is lossless compression, and give an example?
back: Lossless compression shrinks a file without losing any data, so the original can be perfectly rebuilt. Examples: PNG (images), FLAC (audio) and ZIP (files). Used where data must stay perfect.

front: What is a codec?
back: A codec is a program that shrinks (compresses) and expands (decompresses) audio or video so it can be played. Examples: H.264 for video, AAC or MP3 for audio. Without the right codec, a file won't play.

front: Give two implications of choosing a wireless connection over a wired one.
back: Wireless offers freedom to move around without cables. But it's more open to interference, can be less secure (e.g. unsecured Wi-Fi), and is usually slower and less consistent than wired.

front: Name two network components and explain how they affect performance.
back: A router directs data between networks; a slow router creates a bottleneck. A switch connects devices within a LAN; a managed switch can prioritise important traffic (Quality of Service) to keep key apps fast.

front: What is a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attack in data transmission?
back: A man-in-the-middle (MitM) attack is when a hacker secretly gets between two people or systems and reads or changes what they send each other. It is a risk on unsecured public Wi-Fi. HTTPS and VPNs help stop it.

front: What is a private cloud?
back: A private cloud is a cloud used by only one organisation, hosted at their site or by another company for them. It gives more control and security than public cloud, but costs more.

front: What is a public cloud?
back: A public cloud is where servers and software are owned and run by a provider (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud) and shared between many customers over the internet.

front: What is a hybrid cloud and why would an organisation use one?
back: A hybrid cloud combines a private and a public cloud so data and apps can move between them. Companies keep sensitive data private while using the cheaper public cloud for the rest.

front: What does IaaS stand for and what does it provide?
back: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — the provider gives you servers, storage and networking; you manage the software. Example: Amazon EC2.

front: What does SaaS stand for and give two examples?
back: SaaS (Software as a Service) — the provider hosts software you use through a web browser, no install needed. Examples: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce.

front: What does PaaS stand for and who uses it?
back: PaaS (Platform as a Service) — a ready-made environment where developers build, test and launch apps without managing the servers underneath. Examples: Google App Engine, Azure App Service.

front: Compare IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS — what does each layer manage?
back: IaaS: provider manages the hardware, you manage the software. PaaS: provider also manages the operating system and platform, you just build the app. SaaS: provider manages everything, you just use the app.

front: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of cloud computing for organisations.
back: Benefits: you can scale up or down instantly, and you pay as you go instead of buying hardware. Drawbacks: you depend on the internet (down if the connection fails), plus security and data location concerns.

front: How does a VPN support remote working?
back: A VPN lets remote workers connect to the office network securely over the internet, through an encrypted tunnel. They can reach files and systems as if they were sitting in the office.

front: What is remote desktop technology?
back: Remote desktop software (like Microsoft Remote Desktop or TeamViewer) lets you view and control another computer's screen over a network. IT support and remote workers use it to reach office computers.

front: What does 'scalability' mean when choosing an online system?
back: Scalability means the system can handle more work by adding more resources. Cloud systems are highly scalable because you can quickly add storage or computing power when needed.

front: Give two implications of social media use for organisations.
back: Good: cheap marketing, brand building and direct contact with customers. Bad: a negative review or staff mistake can go viral and damage the reputation very quickly.

front: What is the difference between a blog and a vlog?
back: A blog is a written online journal or article site. A vlog is the same but in video form, usually hosted on YouTube.

front: What is a wiki and give an example?
back: A wiki is a website that many people can edit together. Wikipedia is the best-known example. Companies use internal wikis to store knowledge and documentation.

front: What is a podcast?
back: A podcast is an audio show you can download or stream and listen to whenever you like, through apps like Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

front: What privacy risks arise for individuals using online communities?
back: Personal details shared on social media can be collected and used for ads, and data breaches can expose private information. Users should use privacy settings and avoid sharing sensitive details.

front: Give two security risks associated with online communities.
back: Phishing tricks people into giving up login details by pretending to be someone they trust. Malicious links shared in forums or messages can install malware on a device.

front: How can online communities both increase and decrease employee productivity?
back: Tools like Microsoft Teams can boost productivity through quick collaboration. But too much social media or chatting during work time can distract staff and cut output.

front: What is an acceptable use policy (AUP) in relation to online communities?
back: An acceptable use policy (AUP) is a written set of rules on how staff may use the company's IT and internet, including social media. It protects the company from legal trouble and misuse.

front: Give two business uses of instant messaging platforms.
back: Instant messaging tools like Teams or Slack let staff chat, call and video in real time. They support remote work and can plug into other business apps.

front: Give two security considerations when selecting a cloud provider.
back: Data should be encrypted (in transit and when stored) so it can't be read if stolen. Data sovereignty — checking data stays in the UK/EU — keeps it compliant with UK GDPR.

front: Why is accessibility an important consideration for online communities?
back: Accessibility means making the site usable by people with disabilities (sight, hearing, motor or thinking). Missing features like captions or screen-reader support could exclude users and break the Equality Act.

front: What is the impact of downtime on an organisation using an online community platform?
back: Downtime means the platform is unavailable, so nobody can communicate or work. It costs productivity and may upset customers. Organisations check a provider's Service Level Agreement (SLA) for uptime promises.

front: How does cloud computing change the cost model for organisations?
back: Cloud shifts costs from buying hardware up-front (CapEx) to paying a subscription or usage fee (OpEx). This helps cash flow and avoids the cost of maintaining old machines.

front: What is an online forum and how is it used?
back: An online forum is a discussion site where people post questions and answers in 'threads'. Examples: Reddit and tech communities. Companies use forums for support and feedback.

front: What is malware?
back: Malware is 'malicious software' — any program designed to damage, disrupt or break into a computer system. Types include viruses, worms, ransomware, spyware and Trojans.

front: What is ransomware?
back: Ransomware locks (encrypts) a victim's files and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, to unlock them. The WannaCry attack (2017) famously hit NHS systems.

front: Difference between a virus and a worm?
back: A virus hangs onto a legitimate file and needs a user to open it to spread. A worm copies itself and spreads automatically across networks without any user action.

front: What is the difference between a white hat and a black hat hacker?
back: A white-hat (ethical) hacker tests systems with permission to find and fix weaknesses. A black-hat hacker breaks in illegally to steal data or cause damage.

front: What is phishing?
back: Phishing sends fake emails or messages pretending to be a real company (bank, HMRC) to trick you into giving away passwords or bank details.

front: What is pretexting in social engineering?
back: Pretexting is when an attacker makes up a believable story to trick you, e.g. pretending to be IT support to get your password.

front: Why are portable devices (e.g. USB drives) considered an internal threat to data?
back: USB drives can be used to copy and remove sensitive data, on purpose or by accident. An infected drive can also spread malware when plugged into a company computer.

front: What is the impact of a data breach on an organisation's public image?
back: A data breach badly damages customer trust, so people leave and revenue drops. There is bad press, lost customers and difficulty attracting new ones — especially if personal data was exposed.

front: What are file permissions and why are they used?
back: File permissions set who can read, write or run a file or folder. Assigning permissions to users or groups limits access to sensitive data and reduces the risk of unauthorised changes.

front: What is the principle of least privilege?
back: Least privilege means users are only given the access they need for their job — nothing more. This limits the damage if their account is compromised.

front: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
back: The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different storage types, with 1 copy stored off-site. This protects against hardware failure, ransomware and disasters.

front: What is multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
back: MFA asks for two or more proofs before letting you in: something you know (password), something you have (phone or token), and something you are (fingerprint). It greatly reduces the risk from stolen passwords.

front: Give three examples of biometric authentication methods.
back: Fingerprint scanning, facial recognition and iris scanning. They use your unique biology to verify who you are, making them much harder to steal than a password.

front: Give two examples of physical access control methods.
back: Swipe cards, PIN-protected doors and CCTV. These block physical entry to server rooms and deter theft, protecting hardware from theft or tampering.

front: What is a digital certificate?
back: A digital certificate is an electronic ID card for a website, issued by a trusted authority. It links a public key to the site's identity and is used to set up encrypted HTTPS.

front: How does antivirus software protect a computer system?
back: Antivirus scans files for known malware and suspicious behaviour. It quarantines or deletes threats, watches in real time, and updates regularly to catch new malware.

front: What is a firewall and how does it protect a network?
back: A firewall watches traffic coming in and out and allows or blocks it using set rules. It stops unauthorised access and blocks harmful traffic. It can be hardware or software.

front: What is encryption and how does it protect stored data?
back: Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable code (ciphertext) using a key. Without the key it can't be read. Full-disk encryption (BitLocker) protects data on lost devices.

front: How does HTTPS encryption protect users of secure websites?
back: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt data between your browser and the site, stopping interception. The padlock in the address bar shows a valid certificate is in use. Needed for logins and shopping.

front: How can natural disasters pose a threat to data?
back: Floods, fires and earthquakes can physically destroy servers, causing permanent data loss. Protect against this with off-site backups, cloud storage and disaster recovery plans.

front: How can a data breach lead to financial loss for an organisation?
back: Fines from the ICO under UK GDPR (up to £17.5 million or 4% of yearly turnover), compensation to victims, and legal costs — plus lost business from reputation damage.

front: Give an example of accidental data disclosure and how to prevent it.
back: An employee accidentally emailing personal data to the wrong person. Prevent it with staff training, email 'delay send', and data loss prevention tools that flag sensitive data.

front: What is an audit log and why is it important for data protection?
back: An audit log is an automatic record of what users do — logins, file access, changes. It helps spot suspicious behaviour, investigate incidents, and show regulators the system is compliant.

front: What is spyware?
back: Spyware secretly watches what you do and collects data (keystrokes, browsing, logins) without you knowing, sending it to a third party. It can come from malicious downloads or dodgy websites.

front: Give two examples of accidental damage as a threat to data.
back: Accidentally deleting important files, or a hard drive crash from a knock or power surge. Regular backups and access controls reduce the damage.

front: Give two implications of online retail (e-commerce) for organisations.
back: E-commerce lets shops sell 24/7 around the world, cutting the cost of physical stores. But they must invest in secure payment systems, website upkeep and logistics to compete.

front: Give two features of online banking services.
back: Online banking lets customers check balances, move money and pay bills any time, via website or app. Security includes multi-factor authentication (one-time codes) and device registration.

front: Give two benefits of online education and training for individuals.
back: Flexible access — study at your own pace from anywhere with internet. Wider choice — courses from anywhere in the world, often cheaper than in-person.

front: Give two examples of online entertainment services and their implications.
back: Streaming (Netflix, Spotify) gives on-demand film and music. Online gaming connects players globally. Both raise privacy concerns and can encourage sitting too much.

front: How do online booking systems benefit organisations and customers?
back: Organisations save on admin and bookings go through 24/7 without staff. Customers can instantly check availability, compare prices and confirm bookings.

front: What is transactional data and give two examples of its use.
back: Transactional data records each transaction — purchases, bookings, payments. Retailers use it to spot buying trends and manage stock; banks use it to detect suspicious spending.

front: What is targeted marketing and how is it enabled by IT systems?
back: Targeted marketing uses data to show personalised ads based on browsing, purchases and demographics. Platforms like Facebook Ads and Google Ads match ads to likely buyers.

front: Give two IT tools that support collaborative working and explain how.
back: SharePoint lets teams co-author documents in one place. Google Workspace (Docs/Sheets) lets several people edit the same file at once, with changes tracked.

front: Give two IT systems that enable remote working.
back: VPNs give secure encrypted access to the office network from home. Video tools like Teams and Zoom give meetings and screen sharing without being there in person.

front: What is the difference between primary and secondary data?
back: Primary data is information you collect yourself for a set purpose (surveys, interviews, experiments). Secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else (government stats, reports).

front: Give two methods of ensuring the reliability of information.
back: Check the information against several independent sources, and check the source is trusted and up to date (e.g. government or peer-reviewed).

front: Compare questionnaires and focus groups as methods of data collection.
back: Questionnaires reach many people quickly and cheaply and give numbers. Focus groups are small discussions that give richer detail but cost more and take longer.

front: Why is data accuracy important for organisations?
back: Bad data leads to bad decisions (e.g. ordering too much stock), wasted resources, and legal trouble under UK GDPR. Good data improves efficiency and customer satisfaction.

front: What is data verification?
back: Verification checks data was entered/copied correctly (matches the original). Methods: entering it twice and comparing, or proofreading. It catches typing errors, not whether data is valid.

front: What is data validation and give three validation checks?
back: Validation checks data meets rules before it is accepted. Examples: range check (age 0–120), presence check (field not blank), format check (matches a pattern like a postcode).

front: What does 'ease of use' mean in the context of user interface design for data collection?
back: Ease of use means the interface is easy to understand and navigate. Clear labels, a logical layout and helpful error messages reduce mistakes and training.

front: Give two UI design features that reduce data entry errors.
back: Drop-down menus limit input to set options, stopping typing errors. Input masks force a format (e.g. DD/MM/YYYY). Both cut the need for checking afterwards.

front: Give two implications of online news for individuals.
back: Online news gives instant access to global stories. But misinformation or 'fake news' spreads on social media, so readers must check how trustworthy the source is before sharing.

front: What accessibility features should a data collection UI include?
back: Screen-reader support, enough colour contrast and resizable text, plus keyboard-only navigation for people who can't use a mouse.

front: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using interviews for data collection?
back: Interviews give deep answers and allow follow-ups, producing rich detail. But they're time-consuming, expensive and can be biased, so they don't suit large-scale collection.

front: What is a loyalty card scheme and what data does it generate for retailers?
back: A loyalty card (like Tesco Clubcard) rewards repeat customers and records what each customer buys, when and how often. Retailers use this to tailor offers and manage stock.

front: How does system performance affect a data collection user interface?
back: Slow forms frustrate people and cause errors (like clicking a button twice) or abandoning the form. A fast interface keeps data flowing quickly.

front: Why is compatibility important when designing a data collection interface?
back: The interface must work on different operating systems and browsers (Windows, Mac, Android, iOS; Chrome, Edge, Safari) or some users can't submit data.

front: Give two implications of e-commerce for individuals as consumers.
back: Consumers can compare prices and get things delivered. Risks include online fraud (fake goods, payment scams) and the digital divide for those offline.

front: What is the difference between open and closed survey questions?
back: Closed questions give fixed answers (multiple choice) — easy to count. Open questions allow free text — richer detail but harder to analyse.

front: What moral and ethical issues around privacy arise from the use of IT systems?
back: IT systems gather huge amounts of personal data often without users fully knowing (app location tracking, monitoring). This raises concerns about consent, surveillance and privacy.

front: What are the environmental implications of IT systems?
back: Data centres use lots of electricity, adding to carbon emissions. Making devices uses rare minerals and creates e-waste. Shared cloud computing can be more energy-efficient.

front: What is the digital divide?
back: The digital divide is the gap between people who have internet and technology and those who don't. Causes include cost, location (poor rural broadband), age, disability and digital skills.

front: What is the ethical issue around access to assistive technology?
back: Assistive technology (screen readers, voice input) is essential for disabled people, but it can be expensive or unavailable. This creates an ethical duty to ensure equal access.

front: What is netiquette?
back: Netiquette is a set of informal rules governing polite and respectful online behaviour, covering communication on forums, email, social media, and instant messaging. Examples include not using ALL CAPS (which implies shouting), respecting others' opinions, and not sharing private information without permission.

front: What should an acceptable use policy (AUP) cover?
back: An AUP should specify permitted and prohibited use of IT systems and internet access, rules around social media, requirements for password security, consequences for policy violations, and guidance on reporting incidents. All employees should sign and acknowledge the AUP.

front: What is the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
back: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 is UK legislation that criminalises three offences: (1) unauthorised access to computer material, (2) unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence, and (3) unauthorised modification of computer material (e.g. installing malware).

front: Give an example of an offence under Section 1 and Section 3 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
back: Section 1: Logging into someone else's email account without permission — unauthorised access to computer material. Section 3: Installing ransomware or a virus on a system without authorisation — unauthorised modification of computer material.

front: What is the Data Protection Act 2018?
back: The Data Protection Act (DPA) 2018 is UK legislation that controls how organisations collect, store, and use personal data. It supplements and enforces UK GDPR in domestic law. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is the UK's supervisory authority for data protection.

front: What are the six lawful bases for processing personal data under UK GDPR?
back: Consent • Contract • Legal obligation • Vital interests • Public task • Legitimate interests. Organisations must identify a lawful basis before processing personal data, and document it in their privacy notice.

front: Name five of the seven UK GDPR data protection principles.
back: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency • Purpose limitation (data collected for specific purposes) • Data minimisation (only what is necessary) • Accuracy • Storage limitation (not kept longer than needed) • Integrity and confidentiality (security) • Accountability.

front: What is the 'right to erasure' under UK GDPR?
back: The right to erasure (also known as the 'right to be forgotten') allows individuals to request that an organisation deletes their personal data in certain circumstances, such as when the data is no longer necessary for the original purpose or consent is withdrawn.

topic: F2.1.2 Copyright Designs and Patents Act 1988
front: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protect?
back: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (CDPA) 1988 protects original creative works, including literary, musical, artistic works, films, and software. It gives creators exclusive rights to copy, distribute, or adapt their work. Unauthorised copying is infringement.

front: How does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 apply to computer software?
back: Computer programs are protected as literary works under the CDPA 1988. It is illegal to copy, distribute, or reverse-engineer software without the licence holder's permission. Software licences (e.g. proprietary, open source) define permitted use.

front: What do the Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992 require?
back: The DSE Regulations require employers to carry out workstation risk assessments, provide adequate breaks for DSE users, offer eye tests, and ensure ergonomic equipment (e.g. adjustable chairs, wrist rests). They protect workers from conditions such as RSI and eye strain.

front: Give two health risks associated with prolonged use of display screen equipment (DSE).
back: Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) — pain or injury in hands, wrists, or arms from repetitive keyboard and mouse movements. Eye strain — caused by staring at a screen for extended periods without breaks, leading to headaches, blurred vision, or dry eyes.

front: How does the Equality Act 2010 apply to IT systems?
back: The Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics (e.g. disability, age, gender). In IT, this means organisations must make reasonable adjustments to provide accessible systems and websites, preventing discrimination against users with disabilities.

front: What does the Freedom of Information Act 2000 entitle individuals to?
back: The Freedom of Information (FOI) Act 2000 gives the public the right to request access to information held by public authorities (e.g. government departments, NHS, schools). Authorities must respond within 20 working days and may only withhold information under specified exemptions.

front: What ethical issues arise from organisations monitoring employees' IT usage?
back: Monitoring email, browsing, and keystrokes raises privacy concerns and may damage trust between employer and employee. Organisations have a legitimate interest in security and productivity, but monitoring must be proportionate, disclosed to staff, and compliant with UK GDPR.

front: What is e-waste and why is it an ethical concern?
back: E-waste is discarded electronic devices. It is an ethical concern because devices contain hazardous materials (e.g. lead, mercury) that can pollute if landfilled. Much e-waste from wealthy nations is exported to developing countries, creating health and environmental risks for communities there.

front: What is the ICO and what is its role?
back: The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is the UK's independent authority for data protection and information rights. It enforces UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, investigates complaints, issues guidance, and can impose fines for serious breaches.

front: What is the difference between a single-user licence and a site licence for software?
back: A single-user licence permits one person to install and use software on a specified number of devices. A site licence (multi-user licence) allows an organisation to install software on all machines at a site or within the whole organisation for a single fee.

topic: F1.1.3 Freedom of Speech vs Censorship
front: What ethical tension exists between freedom of speech and censorship online?
back: Freedom of speech allows individuals to express opinions without restriction, but online platforms must also prevent harmful content (e.g. hate speech, misinformation). Organisations and governments face ethical challenges in deciding what content to restrict without infringing on civil liberties.

front: Under UK GDPR, what must an organisation do if it suffers a data breach?
back: If a breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights, the organisation must notify the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware. If the breach is likely to result in high risk to individuals, those individuals must also be informed directly without undue delay.

front: Why should an organisation have an acceptable use policy (AUP) for social media?
back: A social media AUP protects the organisation's reputation by setting clear rules on what employees may post publicly about the organisation, clients, or colleagues. Without one, the organisation may be held liable for defamatory or confidential content posted by staff.
